title: Bigfoot files quietly released by US Forest Service
excerpt: Forest Service records describe reported Bigfoot tracks in Montana and Washington, including an investigation that found signs of a possible hoax.
content:
A missing elk carcass, mysterious tracks in the snow and a suspected hoax are among the accounts described in Bigfoot-related records released recently by the U.S. Forest Service.

The records, released Oct. 15, include a history of Montana’s Petty Creek, a 1982 investigation in Oregon’s Umatilla National Forest and a 2003 Montana newspaper article. They document reports of unusual tracks and the doubts of investigators, but do not establish that Bigfoot exists.

A missing elk and tracks in the snow

In his history of Petty Creek, Leo T. Kinney described a 1949 trip to retrieve an elk carcass with three other people. When they arrived, he wrote, only the entrails remained.

Kinney said large tracks led away through the snow. He believed whatever made them had carried the carcass clear of the ground. The group followed the tracks for about half a mile before stopping.

The following year, Kinney wrote, W.W. Schmitz found similar tracks in the same general area, smelled a strong odor and heard grunting. Kinney said no one saw the creature in either encounter.

Investigators examined 15-inch tracks

In 1982, Forest Service investigators photographed tracks and made plaster casts at two sites in the Mill Creek watershed of the Umatilla National Forest. One print was described as roughly 15 inches long and 7 inches wide.

Wildlife biologist Rodney Johnson concluded that the tracks were not made by a large, two-legged creature. He noted that the impressions were shallower than the investigators’ boot prints, appeared and disappeared abruptly, and maintained a roughly 4-foot stride on different slopes.

Johnson said that if the tracks were faked, someone had gone to considerable trouble.

Border Patrol tracker Joel Hardin was more direct. In a July 28 memo, he called the tracks “a very clever attempt” at a hoax and suggested someone had used a foot coated in soft plaster or rubber. His assessment did not establish who made the tracks.

Montana newspaper reported larger prints

A Jan. 15, 2003, Clark Fork Valley Press article described hundreds of tracks reported near River Road West in Montana. One measured about 16½ inches long and 8½ inches wide, with an average stride of about 5 feet, the newspaper reported. Rain reportedly washed away most of the tracks the next day.

Some witnesses believed the tracks were genuine. One estimated that the animal weighed 800 to 1,000 pounds based on a print, though the weight was not measured.

The newspaper also noted that there was no solid, conclusive evidence that Sasquatch exists.

Source notes: Kinney, Petty Creek history, p. 3; Umatilla investigation, pp. 1–3, conclusions and July 28 memo; Clark Fork Valley Press, Jan. 15, 2003, pp. 1–2. Article based on the supplied draft; original records and release date should be verified before publication.
